prompt: Which part of Node runs your JavaScript?

choices.text: libuv's thread pool
choices.why: The pool never runs JavaScript; it does C work underneath some functions.

choices.text: The operating system's epoll
choices.why: epoll watches sockets; it runs nothing of yours.

choices.text: The C++ bindings
choices.why: The bindings are where a call leaves JavaScript, not where it runs.

choices.text: V8
choices.why: Right. It compiles and runs it, on the main thread.

prompt: "Node is single-threaded." How true is that, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Entirely true: the whole process has exactly one thread
choices.why: `threads.js` counted 7 at start and 11 after a file read.

choices.text: False: each request gets its own thread
choices.why: That is the model Node does not use.

choices.text: Your code runs on one; the process has several
choices.why: Right. V8's helpers and the pool are threads too.

choices.text: True only on Windows
choices.why: The model is the same on every system.

prompt: The C library that gives Node its event loop and thread pool is called ___.
javascript lesson 13 said the microtask queue is emptied when. Which statement is it?

choices.text: Completely, after every task
choices.why: Right, and in Node after every callback.

choices.text: Once per second
choices.why: Nothing about the queue is timed.

choices.text: Only when the program ends
choices.why: Promise callbacks would then never run in a server.

choices.text: Whenever the task queue is empty
choices.why: It does not wait for the task queue to empty.

prompt: What does this lesson add to the model from javascript lesson 13?

choices.text: Several task queues, visited in a fixed order
choices.why: Right. Those are the phases.

choices.text: Code can now run while other code runs
choices.why: Still one call stack, still one thing at a time.

choices.text: Microtasks run before synchronous code in Node
choices.why: Synchronous code always runs first.

choices.text: The browser's model was wrong for Node and is replaced here
choices.why: It is still right; this adds detail to one part of it.

prompt: Put the four phases in the order the loop visits them, starting from timers.
Inside an `fs.readFile` callback, a program calls `setTimeout(f, 0)` and then `setImmediate(g)`. Which runs first?

choices.text: `f`, because it was scheduled first
choices.why: The order of the calls does not decide; the phases do.

choices.text: `g`: check comes straight after poll
choices.why: Right. Timers only come round after check.

choices.text: It changes from run to run
choices.why: That is the case at the top of a file, not inside I/O.

choices.text: Both at once, on two threads
choices.why: Callbacks never run at the same time.

prompt: `race.js` printed `immediate timeout` twenty times out of twenty on one computer. A colleague writes code that depends on that order. What is wrong?

choices.text: Timing decides it there, not a rule
choices.why: Right. Code that needs an order must call one from the other.

choices.text: Nothing: twenty identical runs out of twenty is enough evidence
choices.why: Five milliseconds of start-up work turned it round every time.

choices.text: setImmediate is deprecated
choices.why: It is not; it is the check phase's own function.

choices.text: The timer should have been 1 instead of 0
choices.why: 0 already means 1 millisecond; the question is whether it has passed.

prompt: Where does the loop wait when nothing is due?

choices.text: In poll, until input arrives or a timer is due
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In the timers phase, counting down to the next timer
choices.why: It does not count; it sleeps until the system wakes it.

choices.text: In the check phase
choices.why: check runs setImmediate callbacks and moves on.

choices.text: It never waits; it spins
choices.why: A spinning loop would use a whole processor while idle.

prompt: In `ticks.js`, put what printed in order.
hint: The numbers were written to match.

prompt: In `starve.js` the timer was due after one millisecond. After how many ticks did it run?
A function sometimes calls its callback at once and sometimes after a network request. What does deferring the first case with `process.nextTick` fix?

choices.text: The network request becomes faster
choices.why: Nothing about the request changes.

choices.text: The callback moves to the thread pool
choices.why: nextTick callbacks run on the main thread.

choices.text: Errors thrown inside the callback are now caught for you
choices.why: nextTick catches nothing.

choices.text: One order, every time
choices.why: Right. The code after the call always runs before the callback.

prompt: How many threads does libuv's pool have unless you change it?

choices.text: One per processor
choices.why: It is fixed, whatever the processor count.

choices.text: One per request
choices.why: That would be a thread per request again.

choices.text: None until `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` is set
choices.why: The pool exists by default, created on first use.

choices.text: Four
choices.why: Right.

prompt: Which of these wait for a thread from the pool? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: `fs.readFile`
choices.why: Right. Most of node:fs.

choices.text: `crypto.pbkdf2`
choices.why: Right. It is long pure computation.

choices.text: Reading data from a socket
choices.why: Sockets are watched by epoll, with no thread.

choices.text: `dns.lookup` for a host name
choices.why: Right. The system's resolver blocks.

choices.text: A `setTimeout` callback
choices.why: Timers are kept by the loop itself.

prompt: `node pool.js 6` with the default pool. How many hashes finished in the second wave?
On a four-processor computer, raising `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` from 4 to 6 did not make six password hashes finish sooner. Why?

choices.text: The variable is ignored once the program starts
choices.why: It was set before start, and all six started at once.

choices.text: The pool cannot go above four threads
choices.why: It goes up to 1024.

choices.text: Six computing threads shared four processors
choices.why: Right. More threads help work that waits, not work that computes.

choices.text: pbkdf2 runs on the main thread
choices.why: The callback form runs on the pool.

prompt: 100 requests each waiting a second. How long did `threads.js` take to get all the replies?

choices.text: About 100 seconds
choices.why: That would be one at a time.

choices.text: About 25 seconds, four at a time
choices.why: Sockets do not use the four pool threads.

choices.text: A little over one second
choices.why: Right. All hundred waited together.

choices.text: Under a millisecond
choices.why: Each reply was held for a second.

prompt: Why did the thread count go from 7 to 11 after one `fs.readFile`?

choices.text: Each file opened gets a thread of its own
choices.why: It went up once, by four, the pool's size.

choices.text: The hundred requests left threads behind
choices.why: The count was still 7 after them.

choices.text: libuv started its pool of four on first use
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: V8 started collecting garbage
choices.why: V8's threads were already in the 7.

prompt: `threads.js` used `127.0.0.1` rather than `localhost`. What would a name have changed in its numbers?

choices.text: Nothing at all: names are resolved by epoll
choices.why: epoll watches sockets; it does not resolve names.

choices.text: The replies would have been refused
choices.why: localhost reaches the same server.

choices.text: The lookups would have used the pool, so its threads would appear earlier
choices.why: Right. dns.lookup is on the pool.

choices.text: Each request would have opened a new process
choices.why: Name lookups do not start processes.

prompt: Behind `/slow`, roughly how many seconds did `/fast` take? Round to the nearest whole second.
What does `monitorEventLoopDelay` measure?

choices.text: How late its own timers fire
choices.why: Right. A late timer means code held the thread.

choices.text: How long each request took
choices.why: That is what curl's `-w` measured from outside.

choices.text: How busy the thread pool is
choices.why: The pool can be busy while the loop is free.

choices.text: How many callbacks are waiting
choices.why: It counts no queue; it times a timer.

prompt: A report route sorts 500,000 rows in memory and every other route slows down while it runs. Which fix keeps the sort and frees the other routes?

choices.text: Wrap the sort in `async function`
choices.why: An async function still runs its synchronous code on the main thread.

choices.text: Raise `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`
choices.why: The sort is JavaScript, and the pool never runs JavaScript.

choices.text: Call it with `process.nextTick`
choices.why: It would run a moment later and block just as long.

choices.text: Run the sort in a worker thread
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10.

prompt: Where is `fs.readFileSync` harmless?

choices.text: Inside a request handler, if the file is small
choices.why: A small file on a slow disk still holds every request.

choices.text: At start-up
choices.why: Right. Nothing else is waiting yet.

choices.text: Inside a promise callback
choices.why: That is still the main thread.

choices.text: Nowhere; it is deprecated
choices.why: It is stable and has a proper use.

prompt: How many warnings did one request to `motd.js` print under `--trace-sync-io`?
`--trace-sync-io` prints nothing for your server. What may you conclude?

choices.text: That no request handler anywhere in it blocks on a file
choices.why: `motd-utf8.js` blocked on every request and printed nothing.

choices.text: Little: its silence is not proof
choices.why: Right. Only the calls it watches did not happen.

choices.text: The server uses only the promise API
choices.why: A utf8 readFileSync is invisible to it.

choices.text: The flag is broken in Node 22
choices.why: It caught the Buffer form four times.

prompt: When does a Node process exit on its own?

choices.text: When the last line of the file has run to the end
choices.why: `alive.js` printed its last line and went on ticking.

choices.text: After one minute without requests
choices.why: No timeout like that exists.

choices.text: When `beforeExit` is emitted
choices.why: A handler there can schedule more work and keep it alive.

choices.text: When nothing is left to wait for
choices.why: Right.

prompt: `timeout 3.5 node alive.js` ended it after three ticks. Why did neither `beforeExit` nor `exit` print?

choices.text: They only fire with `unref`
choices.why: They fire whenever the process ends by itself.

choices.text: The process was killed from outside
choices.why: Right. Lesson 10 handles signals.

choices.text: console.log is off after three seconds
choices.why: Nothing turns console.log off.

choices.text: The interval cancelled them
choices.why: An interval cannot cancel an event handler.

prompt: Calling `timer.___()` stops a timer from keeping the process alive.
Since Node 15, what happens by default to a rejected promise nobody handles?

choices.text: It exits with code 1
choices.why: Right. `reject.js`'s timer never ran.

choices.text: A warning is printed and the program carries on regardless
choices.why: That was Node 14 and before.

choices.text: Node retries the promise
choices.why: Node never retries anything for you.

choices.text: It is silently ignored
choices.why: It printed the whole error.

prompt: Which line in `reject.js` is the bug?

choices.text: `loadPrices();` on its own line
choices.why: Right. Every promise is awaited or given a `.catch`.

choices.text: The `throw` inside `loadPrices`, which ends the function early
choices.why: Throwing is a fine way to report a failure.

choices.text: The `setTimeout` on the last line
choices.why: It never got the chance to run.

choices.text: `async` on the function
choices.why: async is what made it a promise; the bug is not handling it.

prompt: An `uncaughtException` handler logs the error and lets the server carry on serving. Why does the lesson say to exit instead?

choices.text: The process is in a state nobody planned for
choices.why: Right. Exit, and let a clean one start.

choices.text: Node forbids a handler that does not exit
choices.why: It allows it; that is the danger.

choices.text: Logging is not possible after an exception
choices.why: The handler logged fine.

choices.text: Exiting makes the error disappear from the logs
choices.why: The point is the opposite: log it, then exit.
